old: Regulates 'deep synthesis' services, meaning deepfakes and other synthetic text, image, audio, video and virtual scenes (25 articles). Providers and technical supporters must verify users' real identities, review content, run security assessments for tools that generate or edit biometric features such as faces and voices, file their algorithms, and conspicuously label synthetic content that could confuse or mislead the public.
new: Regulates internet information services that use 'deep synthesis' technology, defined as the use of deep learning, virtual reality and other generative or synthetic algorithms to produce text, images, audio, video, virtual scenes and other online information (25 articles). Providers must verify users' real identities, review users' inputs and synthesised outputs, and conspicuously label content that may cause public confusion or misidentification. Providers and technical supporters must run security assessments of tools that generate or edit biometric information such as faces and voices. Providers with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must file their algorithms.
reason: Duties now follow the Chinese text. Identity verification (Art. 9), review of inputs and outputs (Art. 10) and labelling (Arts. 16 and 17) bind providers only; the old wording gave them to providers and technical supporters. Security assessments of biometric-editing tools (Art. 15, para. 2, item 1) bind both. Algorithm filing (Art. 19) applies only to providers with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity. 'Deepfakes' (not in the text) replaced by the Art. 23 definition of deep synthesis technology; 'could confuse or mislead' rendered as 'may cause public confusion or misidentification' (可能导致公众混淆或者误认, Art. 17).

old: Guidance from the Ministry of Science and ICT on meeting the transparency duty of Article 31 of Korea's AI Basic Act, in force since 22 January 2026. old: Guidance for the fundamental-rights impact assessment of Article 35 of Korea's AI Basic Act. Operators providing products or services that use high-impact AI are to endeavour to assess in advance their impact on people's fundamental rights, and state bodies must prefer assessed products when they use high-impact AI. The guideline explains the assessment's concept and legal basis and the main considerations at each stage (preparation, assessment, follow-up), and appends a report template, examples of how system functions can infringe rights and FAQs. It presents the assessment as protecting rights while keeping interoperability with regimes such as the EU AI Act.

The guideline explains the concept and legal basis and the main considerations at each stage (preparation, main assessment, follow-up), encourages voluntary assessments for all AI, and appends a report form, examples of how system functions can infringe rights, support information and FAQs.

old: Viet Nam's first dedicated AI law, passed on 10 December 2025 by 429 of 434 deputies present and in force from 1 March 2026. In 8 chapters and 35 articles it governs the research, development, provision, deployment and use of AI systems and the state management of AI; classifies systems as high, medium or low risk, with management measures proportionate to the risk; encourages controlled testing of technology and voluntary compliance mechanisms; prioritises AI in public administration and public services; treats data, computing and safe AI infrastructure as strategic national assets; and excludes AI used solely for national defence, security or cipher purposes.
new: Law of 35 articles on the research, development, provision, deployment and use of AI systems and their state management. It classifies AI systems as high, medium or low risk: providers self-classify and notify medium- and high-risk systems, and high-risk systems need a conformity assessment before use. It prohibits uses such as deception or manipulation causing serious harm and exploiting vulnerable groups; requires disclosure of AI interaction and machine-readable marking and labelling of AI-generated content; sets duties for serious incidents; and provides for a national AI ethics framework and controlled testing. AI used solely for defence, security or cipher purposes is excluded.
reason: Rewritten from the Vietnamese text. The claim that the Law 'treats data, computing and safe AI infrastructure as strategic national assets' misread Art. 5(4), which only makes it state policy to prioritise investment in data and computing infrastructure, safe AI, skilled people and shared AI platforms 'mang tính chiến lược quốc gia' (of national strategic character); that provision is now in notes. 'First dedicated AI law' and the vote count, which the stored Law text does not show, were taken out of the summary (the vote moves to notes). Added from the text: self-classification and notification (Art. 10), conformity assessment (Art. 13), prohibited acts (Art. 7(2)), transparency and labelling (Art. 11), serious incidents (Art. 12), ethics framework (Art. 26), controlled testing (Arts 5, 21).

old: High risk is defined as possible significant harm to life, health, rights, national security or the public interest; medium risk as possible confusion or manipulation of users who do not realise they are interacting with AI or AI-generated content. The official signed text (20 pages, 8 chapters, 35 articles) is published on the Government portal (vanban.chinhphu.vn, document 216334) and in Official Gazette No. 40 of 22 January 2026. Article 1 excludes AI used solely for defence, security and cipher purposes; Article 3 defines developers, providers, deployers, affected persons and 'serious incidents'; Article 4 requires human control and the ability to intervene in every AI decision, system safety and data security; Article 5 promotes controlled testing, risk-proportionate management and voluntary compliance. Article 33 repeals Article 3(9), 4(7), 12(6), point đ of 34(2) and Chapter IV of Law 71/2025/QH15; Article 34 sets entry into force on 1 March 2026; Article 35 gives existing systems 18 months (health, education, finance) or 12 months (others) to comply, during which the state management agency may suspend a system at risk of serious harm. Implementing instruments: Decision 367/QĐ-TTg, Decree 142/2026/NĐ-CP, Circular 05/2026/TT-BKHCN and Decision 33/2026/QĐ-TTg (VN-03 to VN-06). The National Assembly newspaper's report of the vote (daibieunhandan.vn, 10 Dec 2025) was the official source until the signed text was located.
new: Passed by the 15th National Assembly at its 10th session on 10 Dec 2025, with 429 of the 434 deputies present voting in favour, and published in the Official Gazette (Công báo) No. 40. High risk is defined as possible significant harm to life, health, the lawful rights and interests of organisations and individuals, national interests, the public interest or national security; medium risk as the possibility of confusing, influencing or manipulating users who do not recognise that they are interacting with an AI system or with content it generated. Article 4 requires human control and the ability to intervene in all decisions and behaviour of AI systems. Article 5 encourages controlled testing of technology, risk-proportionate management and voluntary compliance mechanisms, and prioritises investment in data and computing infrastructure, safe AI, skilled people and shared AI platforms of national strategic character. Article 27 requires agencies that use AI in state management or public services, and operate a high-risk system or one with significant impact on human rights, social equity or the public interest, to prepare an impact assessment report. Article 29 makes the deployer of a high-risk system that was managed and used lawfully liable for any damage, with recourse against the provider or developer where agreed. Article 33 repeals Article 3(9), 4(7), 12(6), point đ of 34(2) and Chapter IV of Law No. 71/2025/QH15; Article 34 sets entry into force on 1 March 2026; Article 35 gives systems already in operation 18 months (health, education, finance) or 12 months (others) to comply, during which the state management agency may suspend or stop a system at risk of serious harm. Implementing instruments: Decision 367/QĐ-TTg, Decree 142/2026/NĐ-CP, Circular 05/2026/TT-BKHCN and Decision 33/2026/QĐ-TTg (VN-03 to VN-06).

new: Implements the political agreement of 26 June 2025 between the then SVM government (Social Democrats, Venstre and Moderates) and six other parties to create protection against the sharing of digital imitations by amending the Copyright Act. A draft was notified under the EU TRIS procedure as 2025/0654/DK (received 31 October 2025, replacing the withdrawn notification 2025/642/DK; standstill to 3 February 2026, with comments from the Commission). The notified draft would add a Section 73a (personal characteristics) and a Section 65a (performances and artistic presentations) to the Copyright Act, protect both until 50 years after the year of death of the person imitated or the performer, let courts order infringing copies removed from the medium where they are made available, and enter into force on 1 July 2026; its exception did not yet mention danger to life or property. Culture Minister Zenia Stampe introduced the bill on 8 October 2026 and hopes it can enter into force at the turn of the year 2026/27. The bill also changes the rules of the Copyright Licence Tribunal (Ophavsretslicensnævnet) so that the same dispute cannot run before the tribunal and the courts in parallel. The English title is that of the notified draft.

Rodrigo Pacheco on 3 May 2023, with the original ementa 'Dispõe sobre o uso da Inteligência Artificial'; the Senate calls it the 'Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial'. The Senate's Temporary Internal Committee on Artificial Intelligence (CTIA) approved rapporteur Sen. Eduardo Gomes's substitute (Amendment No. 199) on 5 Dec 2024. On 10 Dec 2024 the Senate plenary approved the substitute, which was definitively adopted in the supplementary round without amendments, and the other Senate AI bills joined to it (PL 5051/2019, 5691/2019, 21/2020, 872/2021, 3592/2023, 210/2024 and 266/2024) were declared prejudicados. The text sent to the Chamber is the Senate's autógrafo of the substitute, signed by Senate President Rodrigo Pacheco on 31 Jan 2025; Ofício SF No. 235 of 17 Mar 2025 sent it to the Chamber of Deputies for review under art. 65 of the Federal Constitution. As adopted by the Senate, the law would enter into force 730 days after publication; the bans of art. 13, the rules for general-purpose and generative AI (Chapter IV, Section V) and the copyright rules (Chapter X, Section IV) 180 days after publication, except art. 62, which would apply at once; and Chapter IX on supervision (except the sanctions of art. 50) and Sections III and V of Chapter X on publication. Civil liability for damage caused by AI stays under the Consumer Defence Code and the Civil Code, with the burden of proof reversed when the victim is hyposufficient or proof is excessively burdensome (arts. 35 to 37), and fines are capped at R$50 million per infraction or, for private legal entities, 2% of gross revenue in Brazil (art. 50). In the Chamber the bill is subject to a plenary vote under the priority regime (art. 151, II, of the Chamber's Rules). On 4 Apr 2025 it was distributed to six committees and, because more than four had jurisdiction on the merits, a Special Committee was created; the committee was constituted on 29 Apr 2025 and Dep. Aguinaldo Ribeiro (PP-PB) was designated rapporteur on 20 May 2025. The committee approved requests for public hearings and seminars in 2025, and further bills were attached to the bill in 2025 and 2026, most recently PL 3060/2026 on 1 Sep 2026. Its Chamber status is 'Aguardando Parecer do(a) Relator(a) na Comissão Especial' (awaiting the rapporteur's report in the Special Committee); no report or substitute has been presented in the Chamber, and the last recorded action is of 2 Sep 2026. new: Adopted at Strasbourg on 7 July 2026 and sent to the Council on 8 July 2026 (Council document 11711/26). The plan has three objectives: promoting the safe and responsible use of advanced AI, reinforcing the EU's cybersecurity and resilience, and scaling up Europe's AI capabilities for cybersecurity; the communication sets them out as three pillars, followed by work with like-minded partners. It promotes the implementation of the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Resilience Act, encourages organisations to use AI, including open-source models, to find and fix vulnerabilities, and has ENISA provide guidance and a campaign to secure critical open source software. The Commission will launch an EU Grand Challenge on AI for cybersecurity. Its nine key actions include the EU evaluation capacity for AI models (2027), the access Blueprint and the testing platform (Q4 2026), ENISA guidance on protection against AI-powered threats (from Q3 2026), a pilot Critical Open Source Resilience Campaign (Q4 2026), the Grand Challenge (Q4 2026) and training modules for cybersecurity professionals (Q4 2026). The Blueprint will not introduce new obligations for providers, the evaluation capacity will not be a conformity assessment body, and the testing platform is for testing AI for cyber resilience, not for evaluating general-purpose AI models for compliance with the AI Act. The Commission will set up a working group with ENISA, the European Defence Agency and the Member States on the security risks of frontier AI in defence and dual-use critical systems.
